title: Short Form Video Script Template: 36 Hooks That Stop the Swipe

# Short Form Video Script Template: 36 Hooks That Stop the Swipe

At 0:02, the viewer has already decided whether your video is worth another second. A short form video script template gives that decision a sharper opening: one spoken line, one on-screen idea, then a reason to stay.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you ready-to-adapt openings for TikTok, Reels, and Shorts. Replace the brackets with your own detail, then test the version that makes the clearest promise to a specific viewer.

## Short form video script template: the 30-second shape

Use this sequence when you have one useful point to make:

- **0–3 seconds:** Say the tension or surprise. Put the same idea in short on-screen text.
- **3–10 seconds:** Name the mistake, obstacle, or desired outcome.
- **10–22 seconds:** Give the fix, proof, or three steps.
- **22–30 seconds:** Tell the viewer what to do next.

The opening should make a promise the rest of the video can actually keep. “Here are three ways to…” works when the three ways arrive. “Nobody tells you this” works only if the next line contains something specific.

## Templates for tutorials and how-to videos

1. **Spoken:** “If [task] takes you more than [ADD: time], start here.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Fix [task] first”
2. **Spoken:** “The fastest way to make [result] is not what I expected.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Skip the obvious step”
3. **Spoken:** “Before you buy another [tool], check this setting.”  
   **On-screen text:** “One setting to check”
4. **Spoken:** “I would do [task] in this order if I had to start today.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Start here”
5. **Spoken:** “This is the [task] step people skip, then regret.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Don’t skip this”
6. **Spoken:** “You only need [ADD: number] steps to get [result].”  
   **On-screen text:** “[ADD: number]-step plan”

   **On-screen text:** “Practice this instead”
8. **Spoken:** “Stop doing [common action] before you do [better action].”  
   **On-screen text:** “The order matters”

   **On-screen text:** “What that advice misses”

   **On-screen text:** “Find this mistake”
11. **Spoken:** “You do not need more [thing]. You need a clearer [thing].”  
   **On-screen text:** “More isn’t the answer”
12. **Spoken:** “I stopped blaming [problem] when I noticed this pattern.”  
   **On-screen text:** “The pattern behind it”

## Templates for fitness and wellness creators

13. **Spoken:** “If you quit [routine] in week one, make this change first.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Week one fix”
14. **Spoken:** “Your [exercise] is harder than it needs to be because of this.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Make it easier”
15. **Spoken:** “Beginners: do not copy this part of an advanced routine.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Beginner warning”
16. **Spoken:** “The goal is not [extreme outcome]. The goal is doing this again tomorrow.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Make tomorrow easier”
17. **Spoken:** “Try this [ADD: time]-minute version when motivation disappears.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Low-motivation plan”
18. **Spoken:** “Here is how to make [healthy action] less annoying.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Make it easier to repeat”

## Templates for business, freelance, and creator advice

19. **Spoken:** “A client does not need more options. They need this answer first.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Answer this first”
20. **Spoken:** “If people ask what you do, stop answering with your job title.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Say this instead”
21. **Spoken:** “This proposal line makes [offer] easier to understand.”  
   **On-screen text:** “A clearer proposal”
22. **Spoken:** “Before you lower your price, change this sentence.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Rewrite this line”
23. **Spoken:** “Your content idea is too broad until you can finish this sentence.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Make the idea specific”
24. **Spoken:** “The first question I would ask before selling [offer] is this.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Ask before you pitch”

## Templates for product demos and reviews

25. **Spoken:** “I tested [product] for [ADD: duration] to answer one question.”  
   **On-screen text:** “One question, one test”
26. **Spoken:** “Do not buy [product category] until you know which problem you have.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Pick for your problem”
27. **Spoken:** “This feature matters only if you do [specific use case].”  
   **On-screen text:** “Who needs this?”
28. **Spoken:** “Here is what [product] looks like on a normal [day/task].”  
   **On-screen text:** “A real-use demo”
29. **Spoken:** “The best part of [product] is not the feature on the box.”  
   **On-screen text:** “The useful feature”
30. **Spoken:** “I would choose [option A] over [option B] when [condition].”  
   **On-screen text:** “Choose based on this”

## Templates for stories, opinions, and personal lessons

31. **Spoken:** “I knew [plan] was not working when this happened.”  
   **On-screen text:** “The moment it changed”
32. **Spoken:** “A small [event] changed how I think about [topic].”  
   **On-screen text:** “A better way to see it”
33. **Spoken:** “I was wrong about [topic] for one very practical reason.”  
   **On-screen text:** “Why I changed my mind”
34. **Spoken:** “This is for anyone who keeps putting off [specific action].”  
   **On-screen text:** “If you keep delaying this”
35. **Spoken:** “The hard part of [goal] was not [expected obstacle].”  
   **On-screen text:** “The real hard part”
36. **Spoken:** “I wish I had heard this before my first [project, job, or attempt].”  
   **On-screen text:** “Hear this first”

## How to pick a template

Choose the opening based on what the viewer already feels.

- Use a **mistake** hook when they are frustrated and looking for an explanation.
- Use a **how-to** hook when they want a fast, practical next step.
- Use a **comparison** hook when they are deciding between options.
- Use a **story** hook when the lesson needs context before it can land.
- Use a **beginner** hook when the audience is intimidated by the topic.

Then narrow the line. “Improve your videos” is broad; “fix the first line of your cooking tutorial” tells the right viewer why to stop. A good template is a starting frame, not a substitute for the actual detail in your video.

## How to test the first three seconds

Make two or three versions of the same video opening. Keep the body of the video the same so the hook is the variable you are comparing.

For each version, check:

- Can a viewer understand the topic with the sound off?
- Does the spoken line name a real tension, outcome, or mistake?
- Does the on-screen text repeat the idea in fewer words instead of introducing a second topic?
- Does the next sentence fulfill the opening immediately?
- Would someone in your audience recognize themselves in the line?

If an opening needs a long explanation before the value becomes clear, rewrite it around the first concrete problem. The best hook is not the loudest one; it is the one that gives the right person a reason to continue.

## FAQ

### How long should a short form video hook be?

A hook often fits in the first three seconds. Write one spoken thought, then cut any word that does not clarify the problem, audience, or payoff.

### Should the on-screen text match the spoken hook?

It should support the same idea. Shorten it for scanning rather than adding a separate claim that competes for attention.

### Can I use the same template more than once?

Yes, if the specific problem changes. Keep the structure, but replace the vague brackets with the situation your audience recognizes.

### What should come after the hook?

Move directly into the reason, mistake, demonstration, or first step promised by the opening. The body earns the attention the hook requested.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the input and the returned materials:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
